newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Polish, Czech grains worst hit by floods.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Polish, Czech grains worst hit by floods.

text.p: Grain growers in Poland and the Czech republic face sizeable harvest losses from two-week-old flooding across the region, government and trade sources said.
Polish and Czech farmers will bear the brunt of heavy rainfall in eastern Europe, while Hungary and Romania expect to overcome the problems more easily.
Water levels were subsiding on Monday but emergency teams remained on alert to protect flood walls and clear away damage.
"If it continues to rain....as the delayed harvest finally begins, we might see a fall in the quality of the crops and imports would be necessary," said Polish analyst Michal Kisiel.
He said the government-linked Agriculture Economics Institute assumed grain losses of 500,0000 to 800,000 tonnes, possibly reducing the 1997 grain crop to just 23.6 million.
Poland last year produced 24.7 million tonnes. Consumption is forecast at 26.2 million tonnes and grain reserves amount to four million tonnes.
The harvest will be delayed and the quality will be down.
The Czech Republic's Agricultural Chamber said floods could reduce the grain harvest by 500,000 tonnes to 6.5 million tonnes, as farmers could not get into waterlogged fields.
More rain and delays could cost the country another 200,000 to 500,000 tonnes.
But with 1.3 million tonnes of grain in stock, Czech domestic demand of 6.5 million tonnes may still be satisfied.
Romania, which last week feared rains could impair the quality of its milling wheat crop, today said the adverse weather would not have much bearing on harvesting and exports.

"This year, the good wheat crop has a quality which makes it fit for milling. Consequently it will be sought for export," said Trita Fanita, chairman of the Senate's agriculture commission, in a statement.
Romania expects to harvest 7.07 million tonnes of grain, almost double the level last year, and export 2.4 million.
In Hungary, the wheat crop will be delayed by heavy rainfall and the traditional 60-40 milling wheat to feed wheat ratio could turn into 40-60 due to quality problems.
But the overall grain crop may still be four to 4.5 million tonnes after 3.9 million in 1996 and maize, which likes hot and humid weather, could total more than 1996's six million tonnes.
Germany's key grain growing regions in the north have not been affected by heavy rain, which in many parts of the country brought welcome moisture to light soils.
"Yields and qualities vary but there is no need to assume serious losses or damage," said the ZMP farm price office.
Germany may still exceed 1997's record 42.1 million tonnes harvest by 900,000 tonnes, analysts believe.
Brandenburg state in the country's east is battling with weakened dykes and riverbanks after heavy rainfall.
But the low-lying Oderbruch area, which would be under threat of flooding if the Oder river burst its banks, accounts for only a small percentage of the total grain area.
An analyst said Slovakia, along with the Czech Republic and Poland may need to import grain but Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria may beat western exporters via lower prices.
Ukraine and Russia were also likely grain and oilseeds suppliers to the region and in Poland, a local supply gap in rapeseed may also be offset by imports from Canada.
